difficultyReason: The argument relies on a buried methodological assumption: that the control and treatment populations in the trial were equivalent in ways that matter. The correct weakener attacks this hidden comparability assumption rather than the stated evidence or the conclusion directly. Distractors include a strengthener, an irrelevant epidemiological fact, a choice that attacks only one peripheral premise, and a plausible-sounding but logically inert shift in subject.
stimulus: A large clinical trial found that patients who received the experimental drug Velaprex recovered from moderate pneumonia an average of four days faster than patients who received only supportive care. The trial's researchers concluded that Velaprex directly accelerates the immune clearance of the bacterial pathogen responsible for pneumonia and should therefore be adopted as the standard first-line treatment for the condition.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the researchers' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patients assigned to the Velaprex group were, on average, significantly younger and had fewer pre-existing comorbidities than patients assigned to the supportive-care group.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Velaprex has been shown in laboratory settings to inhibit the replication of the bacterial strain most commonly associated with moderate pneumonia.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several other experimental drugs currently in development target the same bacterial pathway as Velaprex.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Supportive care for pneumonia has improved substantially over the past decade, reducing average recovery times across all patient populations.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some patients in the Velaprex group reported mild gastrointestinal side effects during the course of treatment.

explanations.correct: The researchers conclude Velaprex directly caused faster recovery. But if the Velaprex group was systematically younger and healthier at baseline, the observed difference in recovery times could be entirely explained by those pre-existing differences rather than the drug's effect. This attacks the hidden assumption that the two groups were comparable—the load-bearing methodological premise—and so undermines the causal conclusion without directly negating any stated evidence.
explanations.A: Correct. Introduces a confounding variable (age and comorbidity imbalance) that provides an alternative explanation for the faster recovery, attacking the comparability assumption required to attribute the difference to Velaprex.
explanations.B: Opposite/strengthener trap. Lab evidence of the drug's mechanism of action corroborates the researchers' causal claim that Velaprex directly accelerates immune clearance. This strengthens the conclusion.
explanations.C: Out-of-scope. The existence of competing drugs in development says nothing about whether Velaprex itself works or whether it caused the observed recovery difference.
explanations.D: Too narrow / shift in subject. This fact affects the baseline for the supportive-care group over time but does not explain the difference observed within this single trial where both groups were measured contemporaneously. It leaves the conclusion standing.
explanations.E: Irrelevant trap. Side effects bear on safety or tolerability, not on whether Velaprex caused faster recovery. The conclusion is about efficacy and mechanism, not adverse events.

difficultyReason: A two-step predictive argument in environmental policy. The correct weakener attacks the second link in the causal chain (the move from reduced subsidies to reduced production), which students often overlook because it sounds counterintuitive given economic intuitions. Distractors include a strengthener, a plausible but out-of-scope fact, an answer that weakens only the first link trivially, and a shifted-subject trap about a different sector.
stimulus: An environmental economist testified before a legislative committee: "Fossil fuel subsidies lower the effective production cost for extractors, which inflates output above what markets would otherwise sustain. Eliminating these subsidies will therefore cause fossil fuel production to contract, reducing carbon emissions significantly and moving the country measurably closer to its climate commitments."
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fossil fuel extractors in the country have consistently reported that existing subsidies account for a substantial portion of their operating margins.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Global commodity prices for fossil fuels have risen sharply in recent years and are projected to remain elevated for at least the next decade, making extraction profitable even without subsidies at current output levels.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several neighboring countries have eliminated similar subsidies and subsequently met their carbon-reduction targets ahead of schedule.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Renewable energy sources currently supply less than twenty percent of the country's electricity, limiting their capacity to offset any gap left by reduced fossil fuel output.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Agricultural subsidies in the country have been shown to inflate crop output above market equilibrium in a manner analogous to fossil fuel subsidies.

explanations.correct: The economist's conclusion depends on the chain: subsidy removal → higher effective production cost → reduced output → reduced emissions. Choice B severs the second link: if global commodity prices are high enough to make extraction profitable at current levels even without subsidies, removing subsidies will not cause production to contract. The predicted outcome (reduced emissions) therefore will not follow.
explanations.A: Strengthener trap. Confirming that subsidies represent a large share of operating margins reinforces the premise that removing them would raise costs significantly, bolstering the economist's first causal step.
explanations.B: Correct. Attacks the critical move from 'subsidy removal raises costs' to 'production contracts.' If market prices already compensate, output need not fall, and the emissions-reduction conclusion fails.
explanations.C: Strengthener / opposite trap. Empirical evidence from neighboring countries supports the economist's predicted outcome, strengthening rather than weakening the argument.
explanations.D: Irrelevant / shift in subject. The argument concerns whether fossil fuel production will contract, not whether renewables can fill a gap. Even if renewables cannot substitute, this does not affect whether production will fall after subsidy removal.
explanations.E: Unwarranted analogy trap. The parallel with agricultural subsidies is about a different sector entirely; even if true, it does not address whether fossil fuel output will decline in response to subsidy elimination.

difficultyReason: A methodological argument about linguistic evidence. The correct answer attacks a hidden assumption embedded in a premise—that the metric used to measure language similarity is a reliable proxy for common ancestry—rather than the stated conclusion or any surface-level claim. Students must distinguish this from an answer that weakens only a peripheral premise, an answer that strengthens by ruling out an alternative, and an out-of-scope distractor.
stimulus: A historical linguist argued: "Comparative analysis shows that the Varenic and Dothali language families share an unusually high proportion of cognates—words with common ancestry and similar form—particularly in core vocabulary domains such as kinship terms and numbers. No other known language family shares this degree of lexical overlap with either group. The most plausible explanation is that Varenic and Dothali descended from a single proto-language, implying that the populations that speak them share a common prehistoric origin."
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most calls into question the linguist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Kinship terms and numbers are among the vocabulary domains most resistant to borrowing through cultural contact, making them reliable indicators of genetic language relationship.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Varenic and Dothali populations inhabited adjacent territories for several centuries and maintained extensive trade networks throughout that period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Linguists have not yet reached consensus on the precise threshold of cognate overlap required to establish a definitive genetic relationship between two language families.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several languages outside both families contain a small number of loanwords borrowed from Varenic merchants during the medieval period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Genetic studies of present-day Varenic and Dothali populations have not yet been conducted at sufficient scale to confirm a shared prehistoric ancestry.

explanations.correct: The linguist's argument assumes that high cognate overlap—especially in core vocabulary—must be explained by common descent from a proto-language. But if Varenic and Dothali speakers lived adjacently and traded extensively for centuries, the high overlap could instead reflect sustained contact-induced borrowing rather than shared ancestry. This provides an alternative explanation that undermines the conclusion without denying the observed cognate data.
explanations.A: Strengthener / opposite trap. This choice supports the linguist's methodology by confirming that the chosen vocabulary domains are especially diagnostic of genetic relationship, reinforcing the inference to common descent.
explanations.B: Correct. Offers an alternative causal explanation—prolonged contact and trade—for the observed cognate overlap, undermining the inference that common descent is the most plausible explanation.
explanations.C: Too narrow / irrelevant. The absence of consensus on a precise threshold introduces vagueness about the sufficiency of the evidence but does not offer a competing explanation for the observed overlap. The conclusion is still the most plausible explanation available under this choice.
explanations.D: Shift in subject / irrelevant. Loanwords in outside languages say nothing about why Varenic and Dothali share cognates with each other. This does not address the premise-to-conclusion move.
explanations.E: Irrelevant / out-of-scope. The linguist's conclusion is drawn from linguistic, not genetic, evidence. Noting the absence of genetic confirmation neither attacks the linguistic reasoning nor provides an alternative explanation for the cognate data.
